title: English Grammar Academy
description: A complete, progressive English grammar curriculum from foundational concepts to advanced writing.

lessons.title: Nouns — People, Places, and Things
lessons.explanation: A noun is a word that names a person, place, or thing. Examples: girl, school, book, dog, London. Every sentence needs a noun.
examples: The cat sat on the mat.
London is a beautiful city.
My sister loves reading books.

exercises.sentence: The dog ran across the garden.

quiz.question: How many nouns are in this sentence: 'The teacher gave the children a book'?

lessons.title: Verbs — Action Words
lessons.explanation: A verb is a word that shows an action or state. Examples: run, eat, sleep, think, be, have. Every sentence must have a verb.
examples: The dog barks loudly.
She reads every night.
They are happy.

exercises.sentence: The children played in the park.
The bird sings a beautiful song.

quiz.question: Identify the verb: 'The baby cried all night.'

lessons.title: Adjectives — Describing Words
lessons.explanation: An adjective describes a noun. It tells us what something looks, feels, tastes, smells, or sounds like. Examples: big, red, cold, happy, tall.
examples: The big brown dog barked.
She wore a beautiful blue dress.
The cold, fresh water tasted wonderful.

exercises.sentence: The little girl had curly hair.
He gave her a warm, friendly smile.

quiz.question: How many adjectives: 'The old, tired horse walked slowly'?

lessons.title: Capital Letters and Full Stops
lessons.explanation: Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop (.), exclamation mark (!), or question mark (?). Names of people and places also start with capital letters.
examples: The sun rises in the east.
What is your name?
Look out!
Sarah lives in Paris.

exercises.sentence: the dog ran to the park
exercises.answer: The dog ran to the park.

exercises.sentence: my name is james and i live in london
exercises.answer: My name is James and I live in London.

quiz.question: Which word needs a capital letter?

lessons.title: Pronouns
lessons.explanation: A pronoun replaces a noun to avoid repetition. Personal pronouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they, me, him, her, us, them. Possessive pronouns: my, your, his, her, its, our, their.
examples: Sarah is my friend. She loves sport. (She = Sarah)
Give the book to James. Give it to him. (it = book, him = James)

exercises.instruction: Replace the noun with a pronoun:
exercises.sentence: The boys played football. The boys were tired.
exercises.answer: The boys played football. They were tired.

quiz.question: Choose the correct pronoun: 'Maria and ___ are best friends.' (I/me)

lessons.title: Tenses — Past, Present, Future
lessons.explanation: Tense tells us WHEN something happens. Present tense: 'I walk'. Past tense: 'I walked'. Future tense: 'I will walk'. Regular past tense adds -ed; irregular verbs change form (go→went, eat→ate, see→saw).
examples: Present: She reads every day.
Past: She read the book yesterday.
Future: She will read tomorrow.

exercises.sentence: The children play in the garden.
exercises.answer: The children played in the garden.

lessons.title: Conjunctions
lessons.explanation: Conjunctions join words, phrases, or clauses. Coordinating conjunctions: and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor. Subordinating conjunctions: because, although, when, while, if, since, unless.
examples: I like tea and coffee.
She was tired, but she kept studying.
I stayed home because it was raining.

exercises.instruction: Join these sentences with a conjunction:
exercises.sentence: I was hungry. I didn't eat.
exercises.answer: I was hungry, but I didn't eat.

exercises.sentence: She was happy. She won the prize.
exercises.answer: She was happy because she won the prize.

quiz.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'She ran fast, ___ she missed the bus.'

lessons.title: Adverbs
lessons.explanation: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb. Manner adverbs (how?): quickly, carefully. Time adverbs (when?): yesterday, soon. Place adverbs (where?): here, outside. Many manner adverbs end in -ly.
examples: She ran quickly.
He spoke very loudly.
I will come tomorrow.
The cat sat here.

quiz.question: What question does an adverb of manner answer?

lessons.title: Active and Passive Voice
lessons.explanation: Active voice: the subject does the action. Passive voice: the subject receives the action. Active: 'The dog bit the man.' Passive: 'The man was bitten by the dog.' Passive is formed with the verb 'to be' + past participle.
examples: Active: Shakespeare wrote Hamlet.
Passive: Hamlet was written by Shakespeare.
Active: Scientists discovered a new planet.
Passive: A new planet was discovered by scientists.

exercises.sentence: The chef cooked a delicious meal.
exercises.answer: A delicious meal was cooked by the chef.

exercises.sentence: The window was broken by the ball.

quiz.question: Which sentence is in passive voice?
options: The mouse was chased by the cat.

lessons.title: Direct and Indirect Speech
lessons.explanation: Direct speech quotes the exact words spoken, using inverted commas: She said, 'I am tired.' Indirect (reported) speech reports what was said without quotes, often changing pronouns and tenses: She said that she was tired.
examples: Direct: 'I love reading,' said Tom.
Indirect: Tom said that he loved reading.
Direct: 'Are you coming?' she asked.
Indirect: She asked whether he was coming.

exercises.answer: He said that he was studying hard.

exercises.sentence: She told us that she would arrive at noon.
exercises.answer: 'I will arrive at noon,' she told us.

quiz.question: In reported speech, 'I' usually changes to...
Which sentence uses direct speech correctly?
options: He said that he was hungry.

lessons.title: Clauses and Phrases
lessons.explanation: A clause has a subject and a verb: 'The cat ran.' A phrase does NOT have a verb: 'in the morning', 'under the bed'. A main clause makes sense on its own. A subordinate clause depends on the main clause.
examples: Main clause: The children played outside.
Subordinate clause: although it was cold
Full sentence: The children played outside although it was cold.

lessons.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
lessons.explanation: The verb must agree with its subject in number. Singular subject → singular verb. Plural subject → plural verb. Tricky cases: collective nouns (team is/are), indefinite pronouns (everyone is), compound subjects joined by or (either...or takes the verb matching the nearest subject).
examples: The dog barks. / The dogs bark.
Everyone is welcome. (not 'are')
The team plays well. (collective noun, singular in British English)
Neither the teacher nor the students were ready.

quiz.question: Choose the correct verb: 'The committee ___ decided.'
Choose the correct verb: 'The boys or the teacher ___ responsible.'

lessons.title: Essay Writing — Structure and Argument
lessons.explanation: A strong essay has three parts: Introduction (hook + thesis statement), Body paragraphs (topic sentence + evidence + analysis + link), Conclusion (restate thesis + final thought). Each paragraph makes ONE main point supported by evidence.

structure.introduction: Hook the reader → provide context → state your thesis (main argument).
structure.body: Topic sentence → Evidence (quote, fact, example) → Analysis (explain why this matters) → Link back to thesis.
structure.conclusion: Restate thesis in new words → summarise main points → leave a final thought or call to action.

examples: Essay title: 'Should school uniforms be compulsory?'

Introduction: 'Every morning, millions of students worldwide make the same sartorial choice — their school uniform. But should this choice be compulsory? I argue that uniforms promote equality and focus.'
Body: 'Firstly, uniforms reduce peer pressure regarding fashion. Studies show that...' [evidence] 'This is significant because...' [analysis]
Conclusion: 'In conclusion, the evidence suggests that school uniforms benefit students by... Education should prioritise learning, not fashion.'

quiz.question: The thesis statement belongs in the...
Each body paragraph should focus on...

lessons.title: Punctuation Mastery
lessons.explanation: Advanced punctuation: Semicolon (;) joins two closely related independent clauses. Colon (:) introduces a list or explanation. Dash (—) adds emphasis or an aside. Parentheses (()) add non-essential information. Ellipsis (...) shows omission or trailing thought.
examples: Semicolon: She studied hard; she deserved her success.
Colon: I need three things: time, effort, and focus.
Dash: The exam — which no one expected — was cancelled.
Parentheses: The Eiffel Tower (built in 1889) is in Paris.
Ellipsis: She hesitated... then said yes.

quiz.question: A semicolon is used to...
options: Separate items in a simple list

quiz.question: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
options: There are three options: A, B, or C.
